events.description: Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, assassinated Communist Prime Minister, installed Babrak Karmal
Uprising in Herat
Soviet offensive in Panjsher Valley; Masood evacuated civilians before the last offensive
Konstantin Chernenko replaced Yuriy Andropov as Soviet leader, followed by changes in the Afghan war approach.
Soviets used medium and light bombers from Central Asia for saturation bombing of resistance targets.
Soviets launched their largest operation of the war in the Panjsher Valley with heliborne assaults in Panjsher and Andarab.
Meeting attended by 400 Afghan field commanders at which a senior Soviet adviser accused the Afghan military of cowardice.
Reported spontaneous antiwar demonstrations in Soviet Central Asian cities, triggered by returning coffins.
Reported burning of the military commissariat in Kazan by relatives of killed and wounded.
Sakharov and other dissidents condemned the invasion; Sakharov arrested and exiled to Gorkiy.
Radio announcer Vladimir Danchev altered news broadcasts on Afghanistan.
Moscow lecturer said Islam was a serious internal problem and regime worried about Afghan events' impact on Tajiks.
Soviet spring campaign failed to locate and destroy the Panjsheri resistance, causing recriminations in Moscow.
CIA outlook: fighting expected to increase in intensity over next two years; Soviets likely to add roughly 5,000 to 10,000 specialized troops and use more airpower along borders.
October revolution; subsequent basmachi rebellions against the Bolsheviks in Central Asia lasted until the late 1920s.
A Muslim Red Army appeared in Turkestan in the early 1920s, creating native Muslim militias.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; Moscow combined military pressure with conciliatory policy.
Soviet and Afghan aircraft losses began to increase significantly as insurgents used heavy machineguns and SA-7 missiles.
CIA estimates about 25,000 Soviet casualties (one-third killed), about 67,000 Afghan regime casualties, and over 600 aircraft lost since 1979.
Indirect Soviet military costs of the Afghan campaign estimated at some $16 billion.
The CIA projects the Soviets will add roughly 5,000 to 10,000 troops, mostly specialized forces, in the near term.
The CIA projects that fighting will intensify over the next two years, with more aggressive Soviet tactics and better-armed insurgents.
Sustained Soviet military pressure temporarily reduced civilian support for the resistance in the Panjsher Valley.
Soviet pressure temporarily reduced civilian support for the resistance in Qandahar and Herat.
Soviet offensive into the Panjsher; before it Masood covertly evacuated the civilian population from the valley.
Afghan Government statistics showed insurgents controlled almost twice as many local districts as the government by late 1983.
Sakharov and other dissidents condemned the invasion; Sakharov arrested five days after Western media interview and exiled to Gorkiy.
Spontaneous antiwar demonstrations in Soviet Central Asian cities in response to returning coffins.
Danchev altered official news broadcasts on Afghanistan to express opposition.
Spring 1984 Soviet campaign failed to locate and destroy the Panjsheri resistance.
Soviets launched their largest military operation of the war in the Panjsher Valley and augmented forces by 4,000 men to 110,000.
For several days the Soviets used medium and light bombers from bases in Soviet Central Asia for saturation bombing of resistance targets.
Soviets deployed a second SU-25 attack squadron.
12 SU-25s transferred from Shindand to Bagram.
15 MIG-23s arrived at Qandahar from the USSR.
12 SU-25s arrived at Bagram from the USSR.
A senior Soviet adviser accused the Afghan military of cowardice at a meeting attended by 400 Afghan field commanders.
Konstantin Chernenko replaced Yuriy Andropov as Soviet leader; many changes to Soviet war policy followed.
Soviets found little success in large sweep operations and then switched to small-unit actions.
By late 1981 the Soviets again emphasized large sweep operations after small-unit tactics failed.
Review of Afghan forces after which Sokolov, then First Deputy Defense Minister, commented that Afghan troops were ineffective.
For several days in April 1984 the Soviets for the first time used medium and light bombers from bases in Soviet Central Asia for saturation bombing of resistance targets.
Spring 1984 Panjsher Valley campaign, the Soviets' largest operation of the war, with heliborne assaults and night bombing; most guerrillas and civilians had already left.
Soviets augmented forces by 4,000 men, bringing troop strength to 110,000.
Soviets deployed a second SU-25 attack squadron and upgraded airpower in the Turkestan Military District.
Spring 1984: Army-level radio-intercept regiment deployed to Kabul.
Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, assassinated the Communist Prime Minister and installed a new regime under Babrak Karmal.
CIA assessment estimates ~25,000 Soviet casualties (8,000 killed), 67,000 Afghan Army and 40,000 insurgent casualties; insurgents number 150,000.
Preparations for the Soviet invasion disrupted the civilian economy north of Afghanistan; trucks were commandeered and some factories idled.
A Moscow lecturer told a public audience that Islam was a serious internal problem and the regime was worried about the impact of Afghanistan events on Soviet Tajiks.
Spontaneous short-lived popular demonstrations against the war occurred in Alma Ata, Tashkent, Dushanbe and other Soviet Central Asian cities, in response to returning coffins.
Report that relatives of killed and wounded burned the military commissariat in Kazan.
Sakharov and other dissidents condemned the invasion; Sakharov was arrested five days after his interview with Western media and exiled to Gorkiy.
Moscow Radio announcer Vladimir Danchev altered official news broadcasts on Afghanistan to express opposition to Soviet involvement.
Soviet Union invades Afghanistan, assassinates Communist Prime Minister and installs Babrak Karmal regime.
Uprising in Herat before the Soviet invasion.
Insurgent groups began cooperating in attacks on Kabul.
Soviet military pressure temporarily reduced civilian support in the Panjsher Valley.
Soviet offensive into the Panjsher; Masood evacuated civilians beforehand.
Resistance actions caused temporary but significant shortages of food, fuel and electricity in Kabul.

sources_cited: CIA Intelligence Assessments and Research Papers
key_claims: Insurgents are stronger than at any time since the invasion and have majority popular support.
The Soviets control less territory than in 1980 and have relied on stereotyped search-and-destroy operations.
Insurgent factional rivalries (e.g., Jamiat vs. Hizb-i-Islami) hamper coordination.
Tajik groups, particularly Masood's, are most effective at building cohesive intergroup structures.
Fighting is expected to intensify over the next two years.
The Soviets have been unable to quell the resistance and shoulder most of the combat burden because the Afghan Army is ineffective.
Soviet forces increased to about 110,000 in 1984, with more aircraft, special forces and pressure on Pakistan and Iran to restrict infiltration routes.
The resistance is hampered by tribal and factional rivalries such as Jamiat versus Hizb-i Islami, and lacks unity.
The Afghan military suffers about 30,000 desertions a year and KHAD is plagued by factionalism and disloyalty.
The PDPA Parcham–Khalq split remains unresolved and undermines the regime.
Moscow draws on its basmachi experience but differences in Afghanistan, including outside aid, hinder success.
The Soviets remain unable to resolve the Parcham-Khalq split in the PDPA, the main instrument for Sovietization.
CIA estimates about 25,000 Soviet casualties (one-third killed) and 67,000 Afghan regime casualties since the invasion.
More than 600 Soviet and Afghan aircraft lost since 1979, with losses rising from 1983 due to heavy machine guns and SA-7s.
Direct Soviet military costs 1980-84 about $16 billion; Soviet economic assistance about $1.5 billion.
The Soviet leadership has not been forced to change course; recent promotions of military figures suggest no fundamental dissatisfaction.
Fighting is expected to intensify over the next two years, with Soviet emphasis on interdicting infiltration from Pakistan and Iran and a possibility of incursions into Pakistan or Iran.
The Soviets view most insurgent commanders, except a few like Masood, as lacking disciplined political cadres.
CIA assesses the Soviets are unlikely to make real progress quelling the insurgency, and fighting will intensify over the next two years.
The Soviets are likely to emphasize halting insurgent infiltration from Pakistan and Iran via airpower, informants, sensors and special forces.
A serious challenge to Soviet rule in Kabul would lead to expanded military commitment and a wider war, not a political settlement.
Divisions among Afghans will prevent a unified national organization against the Soviets.
Prospects for a political settlement are dim given Soviet maximalist demands.
The alternative view that the Soviets prevail underestimates insurgent morale and overstates Sovietization progress.
Greater Soviet progress is possible if Pakistan limits its support for the resistance.
